title: Tromsø or Rovaniemi: which is better for the northern lights and a winter trip?
author: Brogan
intro: Tromsø in Arctic Norway and Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland are the two easiest places to reach from the UK for snow, huskies and the northern lights. They're more different than they look, so here's how they compare.
seo_title: Tromsø or Rovaniemi: which is best for northern lights?
seo_description: Tromsø or Rovaniemi? How they compare for northern lights, cold, Santa, husky rides, cost and flights from the UK, and which suits your winter trip.

sections.heading: The short version
sections.text:
- **Choose [Tromsø](/destinations/tromso)** if the northern lights are the main point, you want fjords and mountains, and you'd rather it wasn't brutally cold.
- **Choose [Rovaniemi](/destinations/rovaniemi)** if Santa is part of the plan, you want deep, reliable snow and forest, and you'd like a slightly cheaper trip.

Both need about **four nights** to give you a fair chance of seeing the lights, and both are dark for much of the day in December.

sections.heading: Northern lights: Tromsø has the edge, with a catch
sections.text:
Tromsø sits about 350 km north of the Arctic Circle, right under the band where the aurora is most often overhead. Rovaniemi is right on the Arctic Circle, further south, so the lights usually need to be a little stronger to show up well there.

The catch is the weather. Tromsø is on the coast, and Atlantic weather often brings cloud. Rovaniemi has a drier, more settled inland winter, so clear nights can be more common. In practice, the odds even out more than the map suggests.

What tips it back towards Tromsø is how the tours work. Guides there drive out to wherever the sky is clearest, sometimes a long way inland towards the Finnish border, so a cloudy evening in town doesn't mean a lost night. Rovaniemi tours go out into the forest and to lakes away from the town lights, but over shorter distances.

Wherever you go, the lights are never guaranteed. Book your aurora tour for early in the trip, so you have spare nights if the first one is cloudy.

sections.heading: How cold is it?
sections.text:
This is the biggest practical difference. Thanks to the Gulf Stream, Tromsø is surprisingly mild for somewhere so far north: daytime highs average around -2°C in January, and it's often close to freezing. Rovaniemi is far colder, averaging around -9°C in the day in January, and nights of -20°C or below are normal.

That cold has an upside: Rovaniemi's snow is usually deep, dry and reliable from December to March. Tromsø's coastal snow can be wetter, and a mild spell can bring rain. Tour companies in both lend thermal suits and boots for activities, but you'll still need proper layers, gloves and a hat.

sections.heading: What there is to do
sections.text:
**Tromsø** is a proper small city on an island, with fjords and mountains all around:

- Husky sledding, reindeer visits and Sámi camps in the valleys outside town.
- The Fjellheisen cable car, for a view over the city and fjords.
- Fjord trips, and in some winters, boat trips to see whales feeding further out.
- The Arctic Cathedral and the Polaria aquarium, plus plenty of bars and restaurants.

**Rovaniemi** is built around snow, forest and Christmas:

- Santa Claus Village on the Arctic Circle, open every day of the year and free to enter, plus the ticketed SantaPark.
- Husky and reindeer safaris through the forest, and snowmobile trips on frozen rivers.
- The Arktikum museum about Arctic life, and Ranua Wildlife Park about an hour away.
- Glass-roofed cabins and igloo hotels, if you want to try watching the sky from bed.

If you're travelling with anyone who still believes in Santa, Rovaniemi wins easily. For a couple or group of adults, Tromsø's mix of city, fjords and mountains usually feels more varied.

sections.heading: Daylight and the best months
sections.text:
Both are in the polar night in December, when the sun doesn't come above the horizon in Tromsø at all and only briefly in Rovaniemi. You still get a few hours of soft blue twilight in the middle of the day, which is beautiful, but it limits daytime activities.

- **December:** Christmas atmosphere, the darkest skies and the highest prices, especially in Rovaniemi.
- **January and February:** colder, quieter and often cheaper, with daylight returning fast through February. A good choice for the lights in either place.
- **March:** long, bright days and the best of the snow, while it's still dark enough at night for the aurora.

sections.heading: Cost
sections.text:
Neither is cheap. Norway is one of the most expensive countries in Europe, and Tromsø's restaurants, drinks and tours reflect that. Rovaniemi is also pricey, particularly in December when Christmas demand pushes up flights, hotels and Santa experiences, but day-to-day costs in Finland are usually a little lower than in Norway.

Tours are the biggest cost in both. A husky ride or a northern lights chase can easily cost more per person than a night's hotel, so decide in advance which two or three experiences matter most.

sections.heading: Getting there from the UK
sections.text:
Both have seasonal direct flights from the UK in winter, but the timetables change every year, so check before you plan around them. When we checked in October 2026:

- **Tromsø:** winter flights have been offered from London and Manchester by airlines including Norwegian, easyJet and British Airways. Otherwise, connect through Oslo.
- **Rovaniemi:** seasonal flights run from London and some other UK airports, mostly around December and the new year, and many UK Christmas package trips fly in directly. Otherwise, connect through Helsinki.

Rovaniemi's airport is only about 10 minutes from town and Santa Claus Village. Tromsø's airport is also close to the city, on the same island.

sections.heading: Can you do both?
sections.text:
Yes, if you have a week. Finnair has run winter flights between Tromsø and Rovaniemi, which makes a two-centre trip easy: fjords and the aurora in Norway, then snow, reindeer and Santa in Finland. Check the current timetable.

If you're also weighing other parts of Lapland, our [Rovaniemi, Levi or Saariselkä](/blog/rovaniemi-levi-or-saariselka) comparison covers the quieter Finnish options, and [Lofoten](/destinations/lofoten) and [Reykjavik](/destinations/reykjavik) are good alternatives for the northern lights. For more ideas, see [where to go for a white Christmas](/blog/where-to-go-for-a-white-christmas) or [where to go in January](/destinations/where-to-go-in-january).

Still split? Add both to your [somewhere.party](/) list and let everyone give them points.

faqs.question: Is Tromsø or Rovaniemi better for the northern lights?
faqs.answer: Tromsø is further north, under the main aurora zone, and its tours drive long distances to find clear skies, which gives it a slight edge. Rovaniemi's drier inland weather often means clearer nights, so the difference is smaller than it looks. Neither can guarantee a sighting.

faqs.question: Which is colder, Tromsø or Rovaniemi?
faqs.answer: Rovaniemi, by a long way. Daytime highs in January average around -9°C there, against about -2°C in Tromsø, which is kept milder by the Gulf Stream.

faqs.question: How many nights do you need to see the northern lights?
faqs.answer: Four nights is a sensible minimum. It gives you several chances if some nights are cloudy. Book a guided tour early in your stay so you have back-up nights.

faqs.question: Can you see Santa in Tromsø?
faqs.answer: Not in the way you can in Rovaniemi, which is the official home of Santa Claus, with Santa Claus Village and SantaPark. If meeting Santa matters, choose Rovaniemi or another part of Finnish Lapland.
